<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Memory-Based Advantage Shaping for LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Narjes Nourzad
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>This work was conducted during an internship at Carnegie Mellon University.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Carlee Joe-Wong
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">In environments with sparse or delayed rewards, reinforcement learning (RL) incurs high sample complexity due to the large number of interactions needed for learning.
This limitation has motivated the use of large language models (LLMs) for subgoal discovery and trajectory guidance.
While LLMs can support exploration, frequent reliance on LLM calls raises concerns about scalability and reliability.
We address these challenges by constructing a <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory graph</span> that encodes subgoals and trajectories from both LLM guidance and the agent’s own successful rollouts.
From this graph, we derive a <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">utility function</span> that evaluates how closely the agent’s trajectories align with prior successful strategies.
This utility <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">shapes the advantage function</span>, providing the critic with additional guidance without altering the reward.
Our method relies primarily on offline input and only occasional online queries, avoiding dependence on continuous LLM supervision. Preliminary experiments in benchmark environments show improved sample efficiency and faster early learning compared to baseline RL methods, with final returns comparable to methods that require frequent LLM interaction.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="id2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_align_bottom">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>University of Southern California</p>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p1.2.1" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<p id="p1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">nourzad@usc.edu, cjoewong@andrew.cmu.edu</p>
</div>
  
</div>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Introduction</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved state-of-the-art results across diverse domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nourzad et al. 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, yet its limitations become evident in settings that more closely resemble real-world conditions.
Sparse or delayed rewards, partial observability, and long decision horizons often result in poor sample efficiency and unstable training dynamics.
Large language models (LLMs) can help address these issues by providing high-level priors, suggesting subgoals, and structuring exploration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schoepp et al. 2025</a>)</cite>.
At the same time, LLMs introduce new challenges.
Their outputs may be unreliable, queries can be expensive, and continuous supervision risks diluting the role of environment-driven feedback.
Thus, it is challenging to integrate LLM guidance in a way that enhances RL without creating excessive dependence. The goal is to ensure external signals complement rather than distort optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce an approach that incorporates external guidance into RL models through <span id="Sx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">advantage shaping</span>.
Central to the method is a <span id="Sx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory graph</span> co-constructed from the agent’s rollouts together with offline priors and infrequent online outputs from an LLM.
The graph provides a compact representation of subgoals and task-relevant knowledge that evolves during training, reducing dependence on real-time LLM access.
A utility signal derived from the memory graph is used to softly shape advantage estimates, guiding policy updates and improving early exploration.
The influence of this shaping term becomes asymptotically negligible once the agent’s policy surpasses the usefulness of LLM-derived guidance, ensuring that the convergence guarantees of PPO (proximal policy optimization) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al. 2017</a>)</cite> remain intact.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Methodology</h2>

<figure id="Sx2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17931v1/CameraReady/LaTeX/aaai_whole.png" id="Sx2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:419/201;" width="419" height="201" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Overview of the proposed method.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our method integrates external guidance through a memory graph, initialized with offline LLM priors (e.g., partial trajectory and subgoal decompositions) and augmented with agent rollouts and occasional online queries. Online queries are triggered adaptively when the agent fails to extract useful guidance from memory for several consecutive episodes. The LLM is constrained to the same partial observability as the agent and returns short plans that are either added to the graph or used to bias action preferences through soft logit injection. Formally, the memory graph is given by</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=\Bigl\{\big((o,a)_{\tau_{j}},\zeta_{j},\hat{r}_{j}\big)\Bigr\}_{j=1}^{N}\;\cup\;\bigl\{\kappa_{\ell}\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\;\cup\;\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.502em">∪</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.502em">∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=\Bigl\{\big((o,a)_{\tau_{j}},\zeta_{j},\hat{r}_{j}\big)\Bigr\}_{j=1}^{N}\;\cup\;\bigl\{\kappa_{\ell}\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\;\cup\;\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Each trajectory node <math id="Sx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> consists of a partial observation <math id="Sx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{\tau_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{\tau_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math>, action <math id="Sx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\tau_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\tau_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math>, goal term <math id="Sx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta_{j}\in\{\textsl{g}_{j},\,\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta_{j}\in\{\textsl{g}_{j},\,\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicating a final goal <math id="Sx2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\textsl{g}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\textsl{g}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> or an abstract subgoal <math id="Sx2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}})</annotation></semantics></math>, and estimated reward <math id="Sx2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> for the corresponding action sequence. The second set of nodes <math id="Sx2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\kappa_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\kappa_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> represents subgoals inferred from environment descriptions, while the final term <math id="Sx2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the agent’s target goal(s). These nodes are connected through goal–subgoal relationships provided directly by the LLM.
The graph evolves during training, with new nodes added when novel behaviors are observed and rarely accessed nodes pruned as obsolete to stay keep the structure compact while ensuring consistent guidance with little LLM reliance.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each state-action pair <math id="Sx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(o_{t},a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(o_{t},a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, utility is computed by evaluating the agent’s observed behavior against the memory graph. It leverages the same rollouts used for advantage estimation under the current policy.
Each pair in the trajectory <math id="Sx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau={(o_{t},a_{t})}_{t=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau={(o_{t},a_{t})}_{t=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is compared to a stored trajectory node (<math id="Sx2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>) from the memory graph, aligned with the environment layout in the current rollout. Formally,
<math id="Sx2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}\doteq\hat{r}_{m}\cdot\rho(\textsl{g}_{\triangleright},\zeta_{m})\cdot\mathcal{s}\big((o_{t},a_{t}),(o_{t’},a_{t’})_{\tau_{m}}\big)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≐</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓈</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>’</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>’</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}\doteq\hat{r}_{m}\cdot\rho(\textsl{g}_{\triangleright},\zeta_{m})\cdot\mathcal{s}\big((o_{t},a_{t}),(o_{t’},a_{t’})_{\tau_{m}}\big).</annotation></semantics></math>
The similarity term <math id="Sx2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{s}(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓈</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{s}(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> measures action agreement and how closely the agent’s trajectory follows the path implied by the stored segment (e.g., position or directional overlap).
The factor <math id="Sx2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> serves to downweight matches that are behaviorally similar but pursue different subgoals, computed as the Jaccard similarity between the goals in the rollout and those encoded in memory.
This ensures that utility reflects both behavioral similarity and semantic alignment with successful prior strategies.
Overview of the method in Fig. <a href="#Sx2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Methodology ‣ Memory-Based Advantage Shaping for LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>

<div id="Sx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We incorporate memory-derived utility into the policy update by augmenting the standard advantage term. The advantage function quantifies how favorable an action is relative to the average action at state, reinforcing those with higher-than-expected returns and suppressing those that fall short. However, during early training the critic is poorly calibrated due to limited exploration, often producing near-uniform or noisy value estimates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Henderson et al. 2018</a>)</cite>. As a result, the computed advantages provide weak learning signals, even when the behavior is directed toward the task, leading to inefficient or unstable updates. This issue is more pronounced in sparse-reward or delayed-feedback settings, where <math id="Sx2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> tends to be close to zero for most initial training timesteps. To address this, we define a <span id="Sx2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">shaped advantage</span>
<math id="Sx2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}=A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}\quad\text{where }0&lt;\xi_{t}\leq 1." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mtext>where </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}=A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}\quad\text{where }0&lt;\xi_{t}\leq 1.</annotation></semantics></math>
When critic feedback is weak, <math id="Sx2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> supplies additional direction aligned with task objectives, compensating for flat or noisy gradients and accelerating learning. As training progresses and <math id="Sx2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes more reliable, the contribution of <math id="Sx2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> naturally becomes negligible. Because the utility enters additively and does not modify the reward signal, the optimization dynamics of PPO are preserved, along with its convergence guarantees. More broadly, this mechanism is compatible with policy gradient methods relying on advantage estimation, providing a general way to incorporate structured guidance into RL.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17931v1/main_shaped.png" id="Sx2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:558/395;" width="558" height="395" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Mean return on <span id="Sx2.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake-8x8</span> (top) and <span id="Sx2.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Doorkey</span> (bottom). Our method has the highest return.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Experimental Results</h2>

<section id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method in two environments: <span id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span> (Gymnasium) and <span id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Doorkey</span> (MiniGrid suit), selected to probe early-stage exploration effects and long-horizon, partially observable planning, respectively.
We compare against three baselines: PPO, trained tabula rasa from rewards, Hierarchical RL (HRL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhambri et al. 2024</a>)</cite>, which uses LLM-derived option policies for temporal abstraction, and LLM4Teach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art method where a pre-trained LLM distills guidance into a student RL agent.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Methodology ‣ Memory-Based Advantage Shaping for LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports mean return across environments.
In <span id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span>, shaped advantages achieve faster convergence, but baselines eventually reach the same asymptotic return with sufficient training.
In <span id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>, however, the shaped agent sustains a clear advantage, achieving both higher sample efficiency and stronger final performance. While HRL improves over PPO, it trails our method by nearly a factor of two.
Table <a href="#Sx3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Experimental Setup ‣ Experimental Results ‣ Memory-Based Advantage Shaping for LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports test-time evaluation on unseen seeds for <span id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>.
Here, our method matches the state-of-the-art LLM4Teach in both mean return and success rate, with no statistically significant difference at the <math id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence level.
Unlike teacher-based approaches, however, these gains are achieved without continuous LLM supervision, relying only on limited offline and occasional online queries.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="Sx3.T1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="Sx3.T1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="Sx3.T1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Mean Return</td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Success Rate</td></tr>
<tr id="Sx3.T1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">LLM4teach</td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><math id="Sx3.T1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.912\pm 0.075" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.912</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.075</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.912\pm 0.075</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><math id="Sx3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.970\pm 0.004" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.970</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.970\pm 0.004</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="Sx3.T1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="Sx3.T1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Our method</span></td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><math id="Sx3.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.898\pm 0.093" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.898</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.093</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.898\pm 0.093</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="Sx3.T1.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><math id="Sx3.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.953\pm 0.043" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.953</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.043</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.953\pm 0.043</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Performance comparison on unseen seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SS0.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These results indicate that memory-derived utility provides meaningful guidance in sparse and partially observable environments while minimizing the reliance on expensive LLM queries.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
